sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Medical image interpretation is rate-limiting step in diagnostic care. Diagnostic capacity is distributed far less evenly than disease burden: shortages of radiologists, pathologists and other diagnostic specialists are projected to widen through 2050, and are most acute in the lowand middle-income regions that already carry the heaviest burden [1], so that the standard of interpretation patient receives varies with where, and by whom, they are seen. Closing that gap requires more than assigning label to an image: clinically useful system must reach judgement and express it in terms colleague can act upon, placing perception and language within one model [2, 3]. Where the input is text, this has largely been achieved: large language models encode clinical knowledge at expert level [4, 5] and, once optimized for diagnostic dialogue, produce differential diagnoses more accurate than those of unassisted clinicians [6, 7]. On images, capability has instead accumulated one specialty at time, in retinal imaging [8], dermatology [9] and computational pathology [10, 11, 12, 13, 14], each model trained for single specialty and adapted task by task rather than instructed in language across them. Medical multimodal large language models are intended to unite the two, and report broad gains across image and video tasks [15, 16, 17]. Efforts to organize their assessment around clinician-validated task taxonomies, however, have so far addressed text alone [18, 19]. Progress toward this unification has been rapid. Instruction tuning on image-caption pairs from the biomedical literature first allowed models to answer questions about medical images in natural language [20, 21]. single generalist model then reached competitive performance across radiography, pathology and dermatology [22], and openly released medical model families showed this breadth to rest at least as much on the composition and curation of training data as on architecture [23, 24]. Inputs have since widened from single two-dimensional images to volumetric scans, whole-slide images, procedural videos and serial examinations [25, 26, 27, 28]; outputs, from answers to localized findings and diagnostic reports, are judged by blinded radiologists rather than by benchmark score alone [29, 28]. smaller body of work places interpretation and synthesis in one model, over narrow range of synthesis tasks, and finds the two mutually reinforcing [30, 31]. These gains are uneven across modalities, tasks and settings, and rest on curated datasets under controlled conditions; where image and text are presented together, accuracy tracks the informativeness of the text rather than of the image [32], so how much of reported capability is read from the image at all is seldom established. No such system is yet in routine diagnostic use, and what these models can be relied upon to do across diagnostic pathway, and where that reliability ends, remains undrawn. Establishing effective scaling principles for medical MLLMs presents three challenges: (1) limited data (highquality medical image-text supervision remains scarce and unevenly distributed across specialties, modalities and conditions, while expert curation is costly; expanding training corpora therefore requires maintaining clinical accuracy and diversity as data volume increases [23]); (2) effective adaptation (general-purpose vision-language models provide strong foundation, but translating heterogeneous medical data into specialist capabilities requires careful coordination of visual-language alignment, clinical knowledge acquisition and instruction learning; how to compose and sequence these training signals while preserving general capabilities remains an open design problem [23, 33]); and (3) rigorous evaluation (widely used benchmarks often assess isolated image-question pairs or examination-style cases, incompletely representing clinical workflows that require gathering information, integrating imaging with patient context and making sequential decisions [34, 35, 19]; documented quality defects include erroneous reference answers and questions answerable without inspecting the image [36], while overlap between training corpora and publicly available test data introduces risk of contamination [36, 33]). Addressing these challenges requires scalable data curation, training strategies that integrate complementary sources of medical supervision, and rigorous evaluation grounded in clinical practice. Here we investigate how medical multimodal large language models scale in practice and how well the resulting capabilities generalize across specialties and clinical settings. We introduce Sage-Med-Preview, 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters initialized from Intern-S2-Preview, built by combining stage-specific data curation with progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sage-Med-Preview systematically across public 2 benchmarks and multi-center clinical datasets. Our main contributions are as follows: Scalable medical data curation. We assemble 322.7 million stage-indexed candidate records from over 200 public datasets, over 120 million biomedical literature records derived from 25 million source documents (including PDF documents, books and web pages), and more than 100 private resources. The resulting pool comprises 233.8 million multimodal and 88.9 million text-only records. Through source-aware evidence organization and three stage-specific six-step curation pathways, we construct filtered pools of approximately 93.8 million records for pretraining, 69.6 million for supervised fine-tuning, and 0.3 million for reinforcement learning, spanning 51 fine-grained modality and 31 anatomical categories. We document the composition of each candidate pool, stage-wise retention after filtering, and the data mixtures used for training. Progressive medical multimodal alignment. We develop curriculum combining continual pretraining on 83.8 million records and task-oriented mid-training on 28.1 million records, three-stage progressive supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning with policy-conditioned difficulty sampling and independent reference replay, while retaining general-purpose supervision throughout specialization. Medical pretraining builds medical knowledge and visualsemantic alignment. The three fine-tuning stages then establish instruction alignment, broaden task coverage and refine reasoning-intensive tasks. Adaptive reinforcement learning finally focuses on tasks of informative difficulty and anchors updates to reference answers. Comprehensive evaluation. We evaluate Sage-Med-Preview alongside 77 general-purpose and medical models, comprising 68 open-source and nine proprietary models, on 238 clinical tasks from 61 public benchmarks and 13 private multi-center benchmarks contributed by 14 hospitals and institutions, covering more than 40 modalities under unified test splits and standardized scoring protocols. On the 31 public multimodal benchmarks, this evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs still trail general-purpose MLLMs on 29 of them, which indicates that domain-specific training alone has not yet closed the gap to general foundation models. Sage-Med-Preview narrows this gap: it leads all open-source models on the same 31 benchmarks with an average of 58.26%, and it outperforms the proprietary GPT-6.2-Sol in comprehensive multimodal understanding and report generation while performing comparably in visual grounding. This advantage also holds beyond public data. On the private multi-center benchmarks, Sage-Med-Preview is the strongest of all evaluated models, averaging 57.72% against 51.24% for GPT-6.2-Sol.

sections.title: 2.1 Scaling Medical Training Data to over 300 Million Candidate Records
sections.content: Recent medical visionlanguage foundation models, including MedGemma, Lingshu, Hulu-Med and ClinFusion, have demonstrated the value of combining medical images, biomedical knowledge and task-oriented supervision [24, 23, 27, 28]. Scaling these resources requires preserving evidence across heterogeneous source formats and matching supervision to distinct training objectives, as data composition and quality shape the utility of additional training data [37, 38]. We therefore combined source-aware evidence organization with stage-specific curation to assemble approximately 322.7 million stage-indexed candidate records: 232.8 million for the pretraining (PT) family, 87.4 million for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and 2.5 million for reinforcement learning (RL) (Fig. 3b). The inventory contains approximately 233.8 million multimodal and 88.9 million text-only records. These counts describe candidates before stage-specific filtering, rather than the records used in individual training stages. Record definitions and inventory accounting are detailed in Supplementary Section S1.1.

sections.title: 2.1.1 Data Collection and Source Organization
sections.content: Data sources and integration. We integrated more than 200 public medical datasets, over 120 million biomedical literature records derived from 25 million source documents (including PDF documents, books and web pages), 3 and more than 100 private data resources, spanning imagetext pairs, task collections and specialty imaging resources. As summarized in Fig. 3a, public resources and private corpora were processed through document extraction or dataset integration according to their source structure. For PDF documents and web page files, MinerU [39] extracted text and figures. Existing multimodal collections were standardized by checking media references and imagetext pairing structure, normalizing metadata, and preserving available annotations and source context. Text-only and task-oriented resources were organized while retaining available references, source links and supervision targets. Modality, anatomical and medical-concept metadata were retained where available, supporting subsequent record selection and coverage analysis. Evidence organization and supervision. The two processing routes converged on source-linked evidence: extracted figures were associated with their original legends, in-text references and relevant surrounding passages, whereas standardized dataset records retained their accompanying text, annotations and available source context (Fig. 3a). This evidence supported three curation operations: retaining usable supervision, refining deficient descriptions or responses, and synthesizing additional tasks supported by the source material. The resulting supervision was organized into four groups: image descriptions, question answering and reasoning, report generation, and visual grounding. Report supervision preserved available section structure, such as clinical history, findings and impression, while grounding required appropriate localization references or annotations. Source links were preserved throughout processing, allowing revised and synthesized targets to be checked against the available evidence during stage-specific filtering. Further details on evidence organization and supervision construction are provided in Supplementary Section S1.2.

sections.title: 2.1.2 Stage-specific Data Filtering
sections.content: The organized records and their source evidence supported three distinct six-stage curation pathways (Fig. 3c). PT emphasized medically relevant content and reliable imagetext associations, SFT required accurate instruction response demonstrations, and RL required reliable evaluation targets and informative model outcomes. Each pathway combined exclusion with the applicable revision, verification and routing operations. Intermediate and retained-pool counts in the figure are illustrative estimates; stage-wise accounting is provided in Supplementary Table S2. Pretraining. The PT pathway processed 232.8 million candidate records. First, visual and textual usability checks assessed media accessibility, content readability and record completeness to exclude unusable inputs. Second, medical-content selection retained material relevant to medical or biomedical learning, removing accessible but out-of-domain content. Third, textual and visual deduplication identified repeated and near-identical records to limit redundant supervision, using MinHash-based text retrieval and image difference hashing. Fourth, imagetext consistency assessment checked whether paired descriptions agreed with the associated images and available source context, identifying mismatches and unsupported claims. Fifth, caption rewriting and rechecking addressed descriptions that were incomplete, repetitive or weakly aligned but could be improved using the image, original legend and linked passages. Adequate descriptions were retained unchanged, and revised targets were verified against the source evidence. Sixth, image-quality assessment examined clarity, exposure, contrast, noise and artifacts using modality-specific criteria to exclude images whose degradation compromised interpretation. Textonly records underwent the applicable textual checks and bypassed image-dependent assessments. The pathway is summarized by an estimated retained pool of 93.8 million records. Selection criteria, duplicate detection and caption refinement are detailed in Supplementary Section S1.3. Supervised fine-tuning. The SFT pathway processed 87.4 million candidate instructionresponse records. First, rule-based screening checked required fields, conversation structure, media references and non-empty targets to establish valid training instances. Second, deduplication removed repeated instruction instances to limit redundant demonstrations. Third, language-model-assisted quality scoring assessed medical accuracy, instruction relevance, completeness, logical consistency and evidential support to screen the overall quality of each demonstration. The 4 main scoring branch required score of at least 3 on five-point scale, with source-specific acceptance rules applied in other branches. Fourth, length and format checks assessed whether responses met the tasks length and output requirements, including the required answer representation and structure. Fifth, task and reasoning verification assessed substantive correctness: direct answers were compared with reference targets, structured outputs with required fields, and image-grounded claims with visual evidence or annotations. Explicit reasoning was checked for internal consistency and support for intermediate claims. Sixth, retained-pool consolidation assembled accepted records into common instruction pool for subsequent curriculum selection. The pathway is summarized by an estimated retained pool of 69.6 million records. Scoring criteria and task-verification procedures are provided in Supplementary Section S1.4. Reinforcement learning. The RL pathway processed 2.5 million candidate records. First, prompt and schema checks established valid task specifications and input fields so that candidates could be presented and evaluated consistently. Second, task typing assigned the appropriate task family and evaluator, accounting for differences between closed-answer, open-ended and spatial outputs. Third, reference validation checked evaluation targets against original annotations or supporting source evidence, including numerical units, clinically important findings and spatial references where applicable. This step established the evaluation basis before model performance was used to estimate difficulty. Fourth, blind rollouts and task evaluation measured model performance. The answering model received task inputs without reference targets, which were available only to the evaluator. In the closed-answer branch, eight responses per prompt provided an initial estimate of model-relative difficulty. Fifth, difficulty-based routing prioritized prompts with two to six correct responses, favouring tasks on which the model could succeed but remained inconsistent. Other success-rate groups were routed to further selection, review or capability retention. Sixth, semantic checks and replay routing assessed agreement with reference conclusions and supporting evidence, complementing the earlier task evaluation. Grounding retained task-specific spatial verification, and eligible records were assigned to RL task families or supervised replay. These offline assessments established the initial candidate selection and routing before RL optimization. The figure summarizes the pathway with an estimated retained pool of approximately 0.3 million records. Reference validation, task-specific evaluators and routing rules are detailed in Supplementary Table S7 and Supplementary Section S1.5. Curated data coverage and allocation. After filtering, the annotated image-reference subset of the curated multimodal data spans 15 modality groups (Fig. 3d) and 10 anatomical categories (Fig. 3f). Coverage is broad but uneven, with pathology, MRI and CT the most prevalent modality groups, and head and neck, thorax and abdomen/pelvis the most frequent anatomical categories. Complementary t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) projections visualize local structure in sampled image representations, coloured by modality (Fig. 3e) and anatomical category (Fig. 3g). Category mappings and analysis procedures are detailed in Supplementary Section S1.6. The retained pools provide candidates for subsequent training-stage allocation, with selected record counts reported separately in Supplementary Section S1.7 and Supplementary Table S11.

sections.title: 2.2 Model Architecture and Training
sections.content: Sage-Med was initialized from Intern-S2-Preview, 35-billion-parameter scientific multimodal foundation model [40]. We organized training into medical adaptation, progressive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and adaptive reinforcement learning (RL), progressively shifting the emphasis from medical knowledge and visualsemantic alignment to instruction following and reward-guided policy refinement (Fig. 2c). Medical adaptation combined continual pretraining with task-oriented mid-training. Three successive SFT stages then expanded medical instruction coverage and selectively introduced more demanding supervision, while retaining examples from earlier stages. Finally, adaptive RL allocated rollouts according to the evolving policy, alongside independent reference supervision on medical and general-purpose tasks.

sections.title: 2.2.1 Medical Multimodal Knowledge Pretraining
sections.content: Continual pretraining used 83.8 million records comprising medical imagetext pairs, document-derived evidence, textual medical knowledge and supplementary scientific content. These records were assembled through the source integration and stage-specific filtering procedures described in Section 2.1.2. Image-associated text provided supervision linking visual content to medical descriptions and concepts, whereas text-only records extended coverage of medical terminology and knowledge. This stage provided broad medical-domain exposure before the introduction of more task-oriented training mixtures. Mid-training used 28.1 million records to introduce task structure alongside continued medical and scientific supervision. The mixture combined medical task data and knowledge-and-reasoning examples with sampled pretraining records and general scientific examples. Questionresponse formats increased the emphasis on using knowledge to address explicit requests, while the retained pretraining material maintained broader content coverage. The transition from continual pretraining to mid-training therefore shifted the data mixture towards task-oriented learning before the subsequent SFT curriculum.

sections.title: 2.2.2 Progressive Supervised Fine-tuning
sections.content: Progressive SFT organized medical instruction learning around three successive priorities: instruction alignment, task diversification and selective refinement (Fig. 2c). The curriculum established coverage of medical requests and response formats, expanded image-conditioned tasks, and then introduced targeted supervision for difficult examples and explicit reasoning. Medical and general-purpose supervision were retained across stages, with selected earlier-stage examples incorporated into later mixtures. The reported stage sizes describe complete training mixtures, including replay, and are not mutually exclusive sample counts. Instruction alignment. Stage 1 used 6.1 million records to align medical responses with explicit instructions across text-only, single-image and multi-image inputs. Medical question answering, report generation, visual grounding and selected reasoning tasks linked medical knowledge and visual evidence to different response requirements. The length-stratified medical subset contained approximately 25% short (up to 64 characters), 50% medium-length (65512 characters) and 25% long (more than 512 characters) reference responses, providing supervision across different levels of response detail. Focused questions were paired with concise answers, whereas explanatory tasks supplied more extended responses; conversational examples additionally supervised the use of context across turns. General-purpose examples complemented these medical tasks with broader instructionfollowing supervision. Together, these components established initial coverage of task-appropriate answers, explanations and interactions for the subsequent expansion of multimodal tasks. Task diversification. Stage 2 used 9.6 million records to broaden image-conditioned instruction learning through additional medical visual tasks and task collections. The mixture comprised approximately 60% multimodal and 40% text-only records, combining expanded visual-task supervision with continued text-based instruction learning. Visual tasks required image content to be used according to the request, with reference outputs ranging from focused answers and localization outputs to longer medical descriptions. Medical text and general-purpose examples complemented this supervision with knowledge-based responses and broader instructions. dedicated Stage 1 replay component accounted for approximately 1.6% of the complete mixture, retaining supervision on selected earlier tasks and response formats as additional task collections were introduced. This stage thus broadened medical visual-task coverage while continuing to train on textual instructions and previously introduced requests. Selective refinement. Stage 3 used 6.2 million records to combine targeted supervision for difficult tasks and explicit reasoning with broader medical instruction learning. The mixture comprised approximately 53% multimodal and 47% text-only records, retaining substantial coverage of both image-conditioned and textual tasks. Dedicated difficult-example and chain-of-thought pools accounted for approximately 8.5% and 13% of the complete mixture, respectively. The former concentrated supervision on selected challenging questions, whereas the latter 6 provided intermediate reasoning steps alongside final answers. separate replay component from Stages 1 and 2 contributed approximately 7%, maintaining supervision on earlier tasks alongside broader medical and generalpurpose examples. Direct-answer examples remained part of the mixture, so explicit reasoning supervision was accompanied by continued training on concise responses. The final stage therefore introduced targeted refinement across input modalities while retaining wider range of tasks and response requirements.

sections.title: 2.2.3 Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
sections.content: RL extended reference-based instruction learning through task-specific reward feedback, using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [41]. The framework combined policy-dependent difficulty assessment, task-specific rewards and adaptive sampling with independent reference replay (Fig. 2c). The RL and replay pools each comprised 80% multimodal and 20% text-only examples. Within RL, the task-design quotas were 85% closed-form and 15% open-ended tasks. Initial policy-based assessment classified 14.98% of the assessed prompts as difficult, 73.37% as intermediate or inconsistently solved, and 11.65% as relatively easy. Policy-dependent difficulty and reward assessment. Because prompt difficulty changes as the policy learns, we initialized difficulty estimates from responses generated by the SFT checkpoint and updated them using fresh rollouts during RL. Evaluation followed the supervision available for each task. For closed-form tasks, task-specific verifiers compared responses with reference targets, providing correctness observations for estimating prompt-level success rates. For open-ended tasks, including report generation and explanatory responses, fixed judge applied task-specific rubrics using reference answers and available supporting evidence. These rubrics assessed medical content and evidence agreement, including clinically consequential errors where applicable. Verifier outcomes and rubric scores provided task-specific reward feedback and informed subsequent sampling updates. For difficulty tracking, these assessments were kept separate from auxiliary reward components, so that formatting improvements alone did not indicate improved medical correctness. Adaptive sampling and independent reference replay. Sampling priorities reflected the training signal available under the current policy. For closed-form tasks, smoothed success estimates were used to estimate the probability of obtaining both correct and incorrect responses within rollout group. For open-ended tasks, priorities reflected within-group variation in rubric scores after accounting for judge variability, with uniform sampling retained when reliable calibration was unavailable. Priorities were updated within the four categories defined by multimodal/text-only inputs and closed-form/open-ended tasks, subject to cumulative coverage quotas. Exposure-based downweighting reduced repeated concentration on individual prompts, while uniform exploration component maintained non-zero sampling probability for each prompt. Alongside this adaptive RL stream, independent reference replay supplied teacher-forced supervision on reference responses sampled from separate distribution. Replay remained outside the adaptive RL sampler and did not inherit its sampling weights. The replay loss was combined with the GRPO loss to update the same policy, maintaining direct reference-based supervision as RL sampling priorities evolved.

sections.title: 3.1.1 Benchmarking on 70+ LLMs and MLLMs
sections.content: The core evaluation compares Sage-Med-Preview with 77 LLMs and MLLMs. These models cover the general and medical domains and include 68 open-source and nine proprietary models. By model type, they span autoregressive LLMs and MLLMs, diffusion large language models, and unified understandinggeneration models. SDAR-Chat, Lumina-DiMOO, and MMaDA-Base are diffusion large language models, and all other open-source models are autoregressive models. Model sizes range from 0.182B parameters for BiomedGPT to 1T total parameters for Intern7 S1-Pro. In the general domain, the open-source LLMs are SDAR-Chat [42] and DeepSeek-V3.2 [43]. The general MLLMs include Qwen3-VL in its Instruct and Thinking variants [44], Qwen3.5 at 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B [45], Qwen3.8 [46], InternVL3.5 [47], LLaVA-OneVision [48], LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 [49], MiniCPM-V 2.6 [50, 51], Llama 3.2-Vision [52], and Gemma-4-IT [53]. We also evaluate the scientific multimodal models Intern-S1 [54, 55, 56] and Intern-S2-Preview [40, 40]. The general unified understandinggeneration models are Show-o2 [57], BAGEL [58], Janus-Pro [59], Lumina-DiMOO [60], InternVL-U [61], MMaDA-Base [62, 63], SenseNova-U1 [64], and Lance [65]. In the medical domain, the open-source LLMs are MMed-Llama-3 [66], Baichuan-M3 [67], and AntAngelMed [68]. The medical MLLMs include BiomedGPT [69], LLaVA-Med [20], MedDr [70], HuatuoGPTVision [71], BiMediX2 [72], GMAI-VL [73], MedGemma [74], MedGemma 1.5 [75], Lingshu [23], Hulu-Med [27], and ClinFusion [28]. They also include MedVLM-R1 [76] and QoQ-Med [77], which employ reinforcement learning to enhance medical reasoning capabilities. The medical unified understandinggeneration models are HealthGPT [30] and UniMedVL [31]. The proprietary models are GPT-4o [78], GPT-5.4 [79], Gemini-2.5Flash [80], Claude-Sonnet-4 [81], and Claude-Opus-4.6 [82], together with GPT-6.2-Sol and GPT-6.2-Astra [83], Gemini-4-Argon [84], and Claude-Opus-5.5 [85], which are evaluated on subset of the benchmarks.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Comprehensive Evaluation across Clinical Task Types
sections.content: Benchmarks. The evaluation covers 238 clinical tasks from 74 benchmarks: 222 tasks from 61 public benchmarks and 16 tasks from 13 private benchmarks. Table S12 in Appendix S2.1 gives an overview. These benchmarks together cover more than 40 modalities across medical imaging and clinical text. The 45 core public benchmarks span eleven categories. Five comprehensive multimodal understanding benchmarks, including OmniMedVQA [86] and GMAI-MMBench [87], assess cross-modality image understanding. Two knowledgeintensive understanding benchmarks, MMMU-Med [88] and MMMU Pro-Med [89], test college-level knowledge on medical figures. The multi-frame understanding benchmark MedFrameQA [90] requires reasoning over multiple images, and the medical visual grounding benchmark MedSG-Bench [91] requires localizing targets with bounding boxes. Fifteen specialized multimodal understanding benchmarks, including PathVQA [92], each target single modality or anatomical region. Seven medical reasoning benchmarks, including MedXpertQA [35], test expert-level image and text reasoning. Five comprehensive text understanding benchmarks, including MedQA [93], assess clinical text comprehension. Two medical examination benchmarks, MedMCQA [94] and MMLU-Med [95], test knowledge through multiple-choice questions. Three real-world clinical workflow benchmarks, including MedR-Bench [96], test multi-step clinical decisions. The multilingual understanding benchmark MMedBench [66] evaluates text in multiple languages, and three medical report generation benchmarks, including MIMIC-CXR [97], evaluate chest X-ray reports. The other 16 public benchmarks are ClinHallu [98] for clinical hallucination identification and 15 additional specialized-modality benchmarks described in Appendix S2.3. The private benchmarks, detailed in Appendix S2.2, span ten imaging modalities from 14 hospitals and institutions, covering disease classification, cancer staging, outcome prediction, lesion localization, and report generation. Evaluation protocol. We apply the same inference hyperparameters in Table S15 to all open-source autoregressive models and to proprietary models accessed through their official APIs. Diffusion large language models instead keep the default inference hyperparameters of each model. During inference, we prompt non-reasoning models to answer directly and reasoning models to produce thinking process before the final answer. Appendix S2.6 provides the prompt templates for both model types. After inference, we score model responses on closed-ended benchmarks by accuracy with rule-based matching. On open-ended benchmarks, we follow their official metrics and judge models when these are provided. Otherwise, model performance on open-ended benchmarks is measured by accuracy with GPT-6-Luna-High as the judge model. For report generation, BLEU [99], METEOR [100], and ROUGE [101] measure the semantic similarity between model-generated reports and reference reports, while RaTEScore [102] assesses the clinical correctness of key medical entities in the generated reports. Table S12 in Appendix S2.1 details the metric and judge model of each benchmark.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Performance Patterns across Models and Tasks
sections.content: Medical MLLMs still trail frontier general-purpose foundation models. Domain-specific training has not yet lifted medical MLLMs above general-purpose foundation models, and the gap widens against frontier models. We compare 22 medical MLLMs with 29 general MLLMs, including GPT-6.2-Sol, among 68 multimodal models evaluated on the 45 core public benchmarks. As Fig. 4a shows, the medical group scores lower in all 11 core public categories and on 43 of 45 core public benchmarks, except PathVQA and TemMed-Bench. The largest gaps appear on knowledge and text tasks. Medical MLLMs average 42.71% on knowledge-intensive understanding and 65.00% on comprehensive text understanding, whereas general MLLMs reach 57.12% and 78.14%. Even medical report generation, the category with the smallest gap, shows 49.22% against 52.19%. The gap is larger still for the strongest models. Hulu-Med-235B-A22B averages 59.84% over the 45 core public benchmarks, above every other medical MLLM, whereas GPT-6.2-Sol averages 71.49% and scores lower on only seven of them. GPT-6.2-Sol also exceeds every medical MLLM in nine of 11 core public categories. It scores 86.18% against at most 57.16% on knowledge-intensive understanding and 64.25% against at most 5.65% on medical visual grounding. Open-source general models with far fewer activated parameters already match the strongest medical MLLMs. Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B activates 3B parameters against 22B for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B, yet averages 59.90%. Hulu-Med-235B-A22B wins 17 of their 45 benchmarks. Hulu-Med-30B-A3B has the same 3B activated parameters as Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, yet averages 56.17% against 58.18% and wins 12 of the 45 benchmarks. Among proprietary models outside Fig. 4, GPT-5.4 averages 61.47% against 60.02% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B on their 44 shared core benchmarks. Medical MLLMs hold clear lead only over the previous Qwen3-VL generation. ClinFusion-32B averages 57.34% against 53.85% for Qwen3-VL-Instruct-32B and wins 31 of their 43 shared benchmarks. Domain training thus brings smaller gains than one generation update of general foundation models. Substantial performance heterogeneity across clinical tasks. Beyond the gap between model groups, all models vary widely across task types. As Fig. 4b shows, models score lower on multimodal benchmarks than on text-only benchmarks. The 68 multimodal models average 68.93% on the eight text-only understanding benchmarks but 44.59% on the 24 multimodal understanding benchmarks. Within the multimodal benchmarks, performance declines sharply from comprehensive to specialized categories. The models average 63.02% on five comprehensive multimodal understanding benchmarks, 50.26% on the multi-frame understanding benchmark, and 48.93% on two knowledge-intensive understanding benchmarks. On the 15 specialized multimodal understanding benchmarks, they average 40.09%. Medical visual grounding is the weakest, with an all-model mean of 5.56% on MedSG-Bench. Models score even lower on medical reasoning than on multimodal understanding. The models average 36.36% on the seven medical reasoning benchmarks, below the 44.59% on multimodal understanding and the 68.93% on text-only understanding. On the real-world clinical workflow benchmarks, which require multi-step decisions over whole clinical cases, the average drops to 31.97%. These results reveal two gaps in current training data. First, public medical data still lack high-quality, modality-balanced paired multimodal data [23], leaving models with persistent weaknesses on multimodal understanding tasks. Second, single-turn, complete-information questions and short answers dominate training data, providing little supervision for seeking information or handling uncertainty across turns [6]. Performance biases across model families. Models from the same family, and families from the same team, show consistent strengths and weaknesses across task types. The nine Qwen3-VL models average 80.92% on the eight comprehensive text, medical examination, and multilingual benchmarks in Fig. 4c. On the radiology and pathology VQA benchmarks VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA, however, they average 59.65%, below the 62.86% average of the 22 medical MLLMs. ClinFusion and Lingshu, from Alibaba DAMO Academy, average 75.66% on these three benchmarks, 14.82% above the all-model mean. On the 15 specialized multimodal understanding benchmarks, they average 44.55%, narrowing their lead over the all-model mean to 4.47%. Five Hulu-Med models average 74.30% on these three VQA benchmarks and PMC-VQA but 48.95% on knowledge-intensive 9 understanding. Scaling within family adds mainly text ability, as Fig. 4e shows. Across 10 series, the largest member gains 9.90% on text-only understanding and 12.37% on text-only reasoning over the smallest, but 4.34% on multimodal understanding. These patterns likely reflect training data composition: general corpora with little radiology and pathology VQA for Qwen3-VL, radiology and pathology VQA for the DAMO families, and radiology and biomedical literature figure VQA for Hulu-Med. Reasoning mode does not improve multimodal perception. Reasoning models among general MLLMs achieve substantial gains on text-based reasoning and knowledge tasks but not on image perception, as Fig. 4d shows. The eight reasoning models comprise the Qwen3-VL-Thinking and Intern-S1 series and GPT-6.2-Sol, whereas the 21 non-reasoning models include the Qwen3-VL-Instruct, InternVL3.5, and Gemma-4 series. Across the 45 core public benchmarks, the reasoning group averages 55.35% against 50.81% for the non-reasoning group. The reasoning group scores higher on medical reasoning, comprehensive text understanding, and knowledge-intensive understanding by 9.62%, 7.70%, and 16.01%, respectively, and leads on all 14 benchmarks in these categories. On the four perception categories, however, the two groups show no consistent difference. The reasoning group scores 65.92% against 67.68% on comprehensive multimodal understanding and 50.07% against 53.08% on multi-frame understanding, but 44.22% against 43.08% on specialized multimodal understanding. Its lead on medical visual grounding, 14.86% against 8.43%, comes mainly from GPT-6.2-Sol, which scores 64.25% on MedSG-Bench. The other seven reasoning models average 7.80%. With the 22 perception benchmarks weighted equally, the two groups average 48.09% and 47.55%, difference of only 0.54%. Within the same backbone, enabling the reasoning mode does not improve perception and even weakens it. Across all four Qwen3-VL pairs that share backbone and size, the Thinking variant gains on knowledge-intensive understanding and medical reasoning but loses on comprehensive and specialized multimodal understanding. Among medical MLLMs, the two QoQ-Med-VL reasoning models, built on the same backbones as Lingshu-7B and Lingshu-32B, lose an average of 13.55% on comprehensive multimodal understanding but only 5.35% on medical reasoning.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Results of Sage-Med-Preview
sections.content: Medical multimodal understanding. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms all eight open-source comparators on comprehensive multimodal and knowledge-intensive understanding. We compare Sage-Med-Preview with 12 models in three series. The first series includes four open-source models with 7B to 30B parameters, Qwen3.827B, InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, ClinFusion-8B, and Hulu-Med-30B-A3B. The second includes four open-source models with more than 30B parameters, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, ClinFusion-32B, and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B. The third includes four proprietary models, GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and GPT-6.2-Sol. The rest of this section and Section 3.3 use the same 12 comparators unless stated otherwise. Across the eight benchmarks in three categories, Sage-Med-Preview averages 75.61%, above all eight open-source averages that reach at most 71.46% for ClinFusion-32B. This average also exceeds Claude-Opus-4.6, GPT-5.4, and Gemini-2.5-Flash at 67.74%, 67.22%, and 65.22%, respectively. On the five comprehensive multimodal understanding benchmarks, Sage-Med-Preview averages 80.05% and exceeds all 12 comparators, as the bar charts in Fig. 5a show. Hulu-Med-235B-A22B and GPT-6.2-Sol score 78.37% and 76.81%, respectively. SageMed-Preview reaches 95.54% on OmniMedVQA, above all 12 comparators. On the validation and test splits of GMAI-MMBench, Sage-Med-Preview scores 70.07% and 71.26%, above all eight open-source models and GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.6, and Gemini-2.5-Flash. The radar charts cover knowledge-intensive understanding, multi-frame understanding, and ClinHallu, and Sage-Med-Preview exceeds the 7B to 30B series on all seven axes. The knowledge-intensive mean of Sage-Med-Preview at 69.54% exceeds all eight open-source models, which reach at most 61.64% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B. This mean also exceeds the 67.09% of GPT-5.4. The MedFrameQA score of Sage-Med-Preview at 65.52% exceeds all four proprietary models, including 62.78% for GPT-6.2-Sol. Table 1 lists the full results. Specialized multimodal understanding. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms every open-source model on average across the 15 specialized multimodal understanding benchmarks. Fig. 6ag groups these benchmarks by imaging modality and adds Claude-Opus-5.5, Gemini-4-Argon, and GPT-6.2-Astra to the proprietary series. Sage-Med10 Preview scores 59.81% on the 15-benchmark average, whereas the eight open-source models reach at most 51.62% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B and 51.55% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B. This average also exceeds those of GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-5.5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Claude-Opus-4.6, which reach 54.27%, 52.95%, 48.29%, and 46.94%, respectively. Sage-Med-Preview scores higher than each open-source model on at least 11 of the 15 benchmarks and higher than Claude-Opus-4.6 on 13. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms all eight open-source models on nine benchmarks across five modalities, including Fundus-MMBench and UWF-DR in Fig. 6a, PET-Bench in Fig. 6b, TemMed-Bench in Table 2, MMOral-OPG-Bench and PlaTiF in Fig. 6d, FETAL-GAUGE and SMC-LUD in Fig. 6e, and SurgWound-Bench in Fig. 6g. On two of these, Sage-Med-Preview exceeds all 15 models. For temporal-change assessment across chest X-rays, Sage-Med-Preview scores 46.55% on TemMed-Bench, against 40.01% for GPT-6.2-Sol. For liver lesion classification on B-mode ultrasound, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 99.81% on SMC-LUD, against 72.78% for ClinFusion-8B. The TemMed-Bench subtask table in Fig. 6c shows the source of this advantage. Sage-Med-Preview achieves temporal-change VQA accuracy of 91.15%, exceeding the 83.25% of Gemini-4-Argon. The BLEU-1, ROUGE-L, and METEOR scores of Sage-Med-Preview for report generation exceed those of all 14 models. Table 2 lists the full results. Medical language understanding, knowledge, and hallucination identification. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms all open-source comparators on medical text understanding and identifies clinical hallucinations more accurately than 11 of the 12 comparators. On the eight comprehensive text understanding, medical examination, and multilingual benchmarks in Fig. 7b, c, and f, Sage-Med-Preview averages 89.58%, above the 87.43% of Intern-S2Preview-35B-A3B, the 85.86% of GPT-5.4, and the 85.84% of Claude-Opus-4.6. Sage-Med-Preview surpasses all 12 comparators on PubMedQA and CMB with 81.00% and 92.50%. On the three Chinese benchmarks CMB, CMExam, and CMMLU, Sage-Med-Preview averages 92.35%, above all 12 comparators, including 91.79% for GPT-6.2-Sol and 91.31% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B. Sage-Med-Preview also scores higher than six of the eight open-source models, GPT-5.4, and Gemini-2.5-Flash on all eight benchmarks, and higher than Intern-S2Preview-35B-A3B and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B on seven. On the multilingual medical benchmark MMedBench in Fig. 7f, the Chinese accuracy of Sage-Med-Preview at 96.12% exceeds all 12 comparators, including 94.78% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B. The overall accuracy of Sage-Med-Preview at 91.71% surpasses all eight opensource models, which reach at most 90.01%, as well as the 91.34% of GPT-5.4. On the clinical hallucination identification benchmark ClinHallu, shown in the radar charts of Fig. 5ce, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 77.48%. This score exceeds all eight open-source models, which reach at most 74.76% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, as well as Claude-Opus-4.6, GPT-5.4, and Gemini-2.5-Flash at 76.20%, 75.90%, and 71.63%, respectively. Tables 5 and 6 list the full results. Clinical report generation. Sage-Med-Preview writes chest X-ray reports with more accurate clinical entities than the comparators on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert Plus. We measure clinical correctness with RaTEScore, which compares key medical entities in generated and reference reports. As the table in Fig. 5f shows, the RaTEScore of Sage-Med-Preview at 53.20% on CheXpert Plus exceeds all 12 comparators, with Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B at 53.10%. The RaTEScore of Sage-Med-Preview at 54.63% on MIMIC-CXR surpasses 11 of them. On MIMIC-CXR, the BLEU-3, BLEU-4, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L of Sage-Med-Preview also exceed those of all 12 comparators, with ROUGE-L of 33.37% against 31.90% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B. Averaged over the three benchmarks, the BLEU-3, BLEU-4, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L of Sage-Med-Preview exceed those of all four proprietary models, with mean ROUGE-L of 37.14% against 35.09% for GPT-6.2-Sol. The advantage holds across metrics. Over the 27 pairs of benchmark and metric, Sage-Med-Preview scores higher than Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Hulu-Med-30B-A3B on 26 each, than ClinFusion-32B on 24, than GPT-5.4 on 23, and than Hulu-Med-235B-A22B on 21. Table 7 reports all metrics on the three benchmarks. Medical visual grounding. Sage-Med-Preview localizes findings more accurately than all compared open-source models. Fig. 5b reports mIoU, the mean IoU between predicted and ground-truth boxes, for the six models on MedSG-Bench and on the eight localization tasks of the additional specialized-modality benchmarks in Appendix S2.3. These tasks span ultrasound, CT, MRI, PET, X-ray angiography, colonoscopy, and histopathology. Sage-Med-Preview exceeds the other five models on all nine benchmarks. On the eight localization tasks, Sage11 Med-Preview reaches mean mIoU of 36.45%, against 25.63% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B, 20.28% for ClinFusion-32B, 13.91% and 13.86% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B and Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, respectively, and 5.04% for Lingshu-32B. On renal CT lesion localization in RCC-AID, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 58.20% against at most 27.76% for the other five models. Current models localize poorly on MedSG-Bench. The 68 multimodal models average only 5.56% in ACC@.5, as Fig. 4b shows. On this benchmark, Sage-Med-Preview reaches an ACC@.5 of 30.74%. The eight open-source models reach at most 28.22% for Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B. Sage-Med-Preview also exceeds GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.6, and Gemini-2.5-Flash, which stay at or below 9.57%. At the stricter ACC@.7, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 16.93% against at most 11.55% for the open-source models. Tables 1 and 3 list the full results. Real-world clinical workflow and reasoning. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms the open-source models above 30B parameters on whole-case clinical workflow and exceeds the 7B to 30B series on four of the seven medical reasoning benchmarks. LiveClin follows each case through the clinical stages from assessment to follow-up and credits case only when every question is correct. As Fig. 7d shows, Sage-Med-Preview reaches case accuracy of 47.48% and question accuracy of 84.83%. The above-30B series reaches at most 40.23% and 81.88% for HuluMed-235B-A22B, and Gemini-2.5-Flash reaches 41.22% and 83.16%. Covering examination recommendation, diagnosis, and treatment planning, MedR-Bench evaluates models on clinical cases in single-turn, free-turn, and oracle settings. In Fig. 7e, Sage-Med-Preview achieves OneTurn accuracy of 52.14%, exceeding InternVL3.530B-A3B, ClinFusion-8B, Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B. The OracleTreatment accuracy of Sage-Med-Preview at 29.03% exceeds Qwen3.8-27B, ClinFusion-8B, Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, and ClinFusion-32B. On the seven medical reasoning benchmarks in Fig. 7a, Sage-Med-Preview averages 49.39%, above seven of the eight open-source models, including Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B at 48.97%, Hulu-Med-30B-A3B at 48.85%, and Qwen3.8-27B at 47.21%. The MMLU-Pro-Med score of Sage-Med-Preview at 80.07% exceeds all eight open-source models, GPT-5.4, and Gemini-2.5-Flash. On Medbullets, SuperGPQA-Med, and MedXpertQA, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 75.81%, 59.35%, and 38.53%, whereas the 7B to 30B series reaches at most 71.27%, 48.13%, and 36.82%. Tables 4 and 6 list the full results.

sections.title: 3.3 Multi-center Evaluation on Private Datasets
sections.content: The private evaluation comprises 13 benchmarks with 16 tasks from 14 hospitals and institutions, as Table S13 lists. All benchmarks except PET/CT are isolated from the training data of Sage-Med-Preview at both the institution and the case level, so the unseen results below exclude PET/CT. We compare Sage-Med-Preview with the same 12 comparators as in Section 3.2.2, and Fig. 8 summarizes the results. The 12 unseen understanding tasks yield 14 scores. Only Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B, ClinFusion-32B, and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B have results on Lung-DP and EndoLoc, so we summarize the comparison at two levels. Over the 11 scores of the nine tasks that all 12 comparators complete, Sage-Med-Preview averages 57.72%, above the 51.24% of GPT-6.2-Sol. The other 11 comparators average at most 42.97%. Over all 14 scores, Sage-Med-Preview averages 58.55%, whereas the four comparators with complete results reach at most 45.61%. On five of the 14 scores, Sage-Med-Preview exceeds every comparator with results. Melanoma metastasis outcome prediction. This task requires model to predict the metastasis outcome of each lesion from dermoscopy images. As Fig. 8c shows, Sage-Med-Preview achieves 76.80% and exceeds 11 of the 12 comparators. These include GPT-6.2-Sol at 75.26%, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 74.74%, the similar-sized Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B and Hulu-Med-30B-A3B at 72.94% and 72.42%, respectively, Claude-Opus-4.6 at 71.91%, and GPT-5.4 at 59.79%. Table 8 gives the full results. Fundus disease classification and report generation. This benchmark requires model to classify fundus diseases and to generate fundus report from color fundus photographs. On disease classification in Fig. 8a, Sage-Med-Preview achieves 70.70% and exceeds 10 of the 12 comparators, including Hulu-Med-30B-A3B at 69.60%, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B at 64.10%, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 59.71%, and GPT-5.4 at 57.14%. For report generation in Fig. 8e, the ROUGE-2 of Sage-Med-Preview at 13.79% exceeds all eight open-source models, 12 among which ClinFusion-8B reaches 13.55%. Sage-Med-Preview also surpasses Claude-Opus-4.6 at 11.96% and Gemini-2.5-Flash at 11.16%. Tables 8 and 9 report both tasks. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging. This task, denoted NPC, evaluates nasopharyngeal carcinoma staging on MRI at the slice level and the patient level. On slice-level staging, Sage-Med-Preview achieves 62.70% and exceeds all 12 comparators, including GPT-6.2-Sol at 57.79%, InternVL3.5-30B-A3B at 52.05%, Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 51.97%, and the similar-sized Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B at 50.41%. On patient-level staging, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 49.18% and exceeds 10 of the 12 comparators, including GPT-6.2-Sol at 43.44%, Intern-S2-Preview-35BA3B at 31.15%, and GPT-5.4 at 27.87%. On the two-level average in Fig. 8c, Sage-Med-Preview reaches 55.94%, compared with 50.62% for GPT-6.2-Sol and 49.67% for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. Both tasks appear in Table 8. Orthopedic admission diagnosis. This text-only task, denoted Ortho-Admission, requires model to determine the orthopedic admission diagnosis from EHR notes. Sage-Med-Preview achieves 61.25% and exceeds nine of the 12 comparators, as Fig. 8a shows. These include GPT-5.4 and Gemini-2.5-Flash at 60.00%, Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 58.75%, and Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 55.00%. Table 8 gives the full results. Pneumonia detection and localization. This task requires model to detect pneumonia on chest X-rays and to localize each lesion with bounding box. The evaluation metrics are mIoU and the accuracy at IoU above 0.3, denoted ACC@.3. As Fig. 8d shows, Sage-Med-Preview outperforms 11 of the 12 comparators on both metrics, achieving an ACC@.3 of 61.41% and an mIoU of 44.18%. The open-source models reach at most 56.52% ACC@.3 and 40.92% mIoU, both from Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. Claude-Opus-4.6 reaches 52.17% and 33.86%. Medical MLLMs localize lesions less accurately, as Hulu-Med and ClinFusion stay at or below 30.43% ACC@.3 and 19.69% mIoU. Table 8 gives the full results. Surgical attention region localization. This task, denoted Surg-Attention, requires model to localize the region on which the surgeon focuses in each laparoscopic frame. Sage-Med-Preview outperforms all 12 comparators on both metrics, as Fig. 8d shows. Sage-Med-Preview reaches 78.85% ACC@.3 and 48.50% mIoU, while the strongest comparator, GPT-5.4, reaches 58.90% and 35.06%. The margin over medical MLLMs is larger, since Hulu-Med-30B-A3B and ClinFusion-8B reach ACC@.3 of 42.90% and 38.35%. These results are consistent with the grounding supervision in Section 3.2.2, which transfers from public and in-house data to this unseen surgical setting. Table 8 gives the full results. Ear disease classification. This task requires classifying ear diseases from otoscopic images. As Fig. 8a shows, Sage-Med-Preview achieves 41.40% and exceeds all 12 comparators. Hulu-Med-235B-A22B, Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, and ClinFusion-32B reach 27.95%, 27.10%, and 26.90%, respectively. The general-purpose and proprietary models also score lower, with 26.05% for Qwen3.8-27B, 23.00% for GPT-6.2-Sol, and 22.30% for Gemini-2.5-Flash. Table 8 lists the full results. Intracranial tumor classification. This benchmark requires model to classify the intracranial tumor of each case by integrating several MRI images. Sage-Med-Preview achieves 40.00% and exceeds 10 of the 12 comparators, as shown in Fig. 8a. These include GPT-5.4 at 37.14%, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B and Claude-Opus-4.6 at 34.29%, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 32.86%, and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 30.00%. Table 8 lists the full results. Lung diagnosis and progression and endoscopic location recognition. The first benchmark requires model to diagnose lung diseases on chest X-rays and to assess interval progression between chest X-rays taken at different times, and we denote it Lung-DP. The second requires model to recognize the anatomical location of each endoscopic image from 27 options, and we denote it EndoLoc. Among the comparators, only Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B, ClinFusion-32B, and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B report results on these tasks, so Fig. 8b shows these models alone. On interval progression, Sage-Med-Preview achieves 82.10%, exceeding all four comparators. Hulu-Med-235B-A22B, Hulu-Med-30B-A3B, Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B, and ClinFusion-32B reach 80.86%, 80.25%, 64.81%, and 56.79%, respectively. Table 8 lists the diagnosis and EndoLoc results. Lung CT report generation. This benchmark, denoted Lung-Cancer, requires model to generate CT report for each lung cancer case from several CT images. We assess report quality mainly by RaTEScore, which measures 13 the correctness of clinical entities. Sage-Med-Preview achieves RaTEScore of 66.52% and exceeds nine of the 12 comparators, as Fig. 8e shows. These include Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 66.13%, Qwen3.8-27B at 65.74%, GPT-5.4 at 64.32%, GPT-6.2-Sol at 58.80%, and Claude-Opus-4.6 at 58.56%. Sage-Med-Preview also achieves ROUGE-2 of 13.81%, exceeding nine of the 12 comparators. Table 9 lists all report metrics. Intraoral photograph report generation. This benchmark requires model to generate clinical report from several intraoral photographs of each patient. As Fig. 8e shows, Sage-Med-Preview achieves ROUGE-1 of 32.21%, ROUGE-2 of 8.25%, and ROUGE-L of 28.59%, exceeding all 12 comparators on all three metrics. The comparators reach at most 30.45%, 7.32%, and 26.95%, respectively. Sage-Med-Preview also attains RaTEScore of 54.15%, surpassing all four proprietary models, among which the highest is 53.36% from GPT-5.4. The same score exceeds Intern-S2-Preview-35B-A3B and Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 52.63% and 52.59%, respectively. Sage-Med-Preview reaches BLEU-4 of 1.61%, exceeding 11 of the 12 comparators. All report metrics are listed in Table 9. PET/CT report generation. This benchmark requires model to generate PET/CT report and compares the output with 133 reference reports written by physicians. Sage-Med-Preview achieves BLEU-4 of 7.88% and ROUGE-2 of 13.66%, surpassing 11 of the 12 comparators on both metrics. The RaTEScore of Sage-Med-Preview at 66.90% surpasses 10 of the 12 comparators, including Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 66.28%, GPT-5.4 at 65.44%, Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 64.49%, GPT-6.2-Sol at 64.38%, Claude-Opus-4.6 at 57.27%, and Gemini-2.5-Flash at 46.78%. Table 9 lists all report metrics.

sections.title: 4 Training Analysis
sections.content: Pretraining data composition. Prioritizing informative content and modality balance yielded greater downstream medical performance gains than pretraining on the full data pool. Standard continual pretraining (CPT) used the full pretraining dataset, whereas refined CPT used selected 30-million-record subset with more balanced modality distribution. Both recipes were followed by the same SFT1 supervision, allowing their downstream utility to be compared after common instruction-alignment stage. All evaluations in Fig. 9ad use the same 20 benchmarks, comprising 14 multimodal and six text-only benchmarks, with performance summarized by the macro-average across benchmarks. Standard CPT followed by SFT1 increased the macro-average from 56.33 for the base model to 61.26, while refined CPT reached 62.82, exceeding the full-data recipe by 1.56 percentage points (Fig. 9a). The stronger performance of the smaller mixture highlights the value of increasing information density and balancing complementary sources of medical supervision. For heterogeneous medical corpora, these findings favor improving content selection and modality composition before further expanding data volume. Progressive supervised and reinforcement learning. Targeted supervised refinement and subsequent RL contributed most of the improvement achieved after initial instruction alignment. Following CPT and SFT1, the macro-average increased from 61.26 to 61.45 after SFT2 and to 62.02 after SFT3, corresponding to successive gains of 0.19 and 0.57 percentage points. RL then raised performance to 63.03, adding further 1.01 points and bringing the cumulative improvement over SFT1 to 1.77 points (Fig. 9b). The larger increments during targeted refinement and reward optimization indicate that substantial scope for improvement remained after broad instruction learning and task expansion. In particular, the additional gain from RL demonstrates the continued utility of task-specific reward feedback after three supervised stages. These results motivate progressive curriculum in which successive stages develop task coverage, refine performance through focused supervision and further improve responses through reward-based optimization. The training-loss trajectory of Sage-Med-Preview-35B-A3B provides complementary view of this process across pretraining, mid-training and SFT (Fig. 9e). Loss generally decreased within individual phases, with changes at stage boundaries followed by further reduction under the next training recipe. Base-model initialization. The performance advantage of Intern-S2-Preview persisted across all three SFT 14 stages, showing that initialization continued to shape the level of medical capability reached after adaptation. InternS2-Preview initialization exceeded Qwen3.5-35B-A3B initialization by 4.31, 2.54 and 2.72 percentage points after SFT1, SFT2 and SFT3, respectively (Fig. 9c). Across these stages, the Intern-initialized model improved from 61.26 to 62.02, while the Qwen-initialized model improved from 56.95 to 59.30. The Qwen-initialized model gained 2.35 points between SFT1 and SFT3, compared with 0.76 points for the Intern-initialized model, narrowing the gap while retaining lower final macro-average. This trajectory distinguishes the capacity to improve during adaptation from the capability ultimately achieved. Evaluating initialization choices across successive checkpoints therefore captures both responsiveness to further training and the performance attainable under the medical curriculum. The consistently stronger adapted performance of Intern-S2-Preview supports its selection as the base model for Sage-Med. Modality and response-length composition. Greater text coverage within multimodal-majority mixture and an intermediate short-answer share improved medical instruction alignment in the respective pilot experiments. For Qwen3-VL-8B, increasing the text share from 29.4% to 38%, with the multimodal share changing from 70.6% to 62%, raised the 20-benchmark macro-average from 48.70 to 49.79, gain of 1.09 percentage points (Fig. 9d, left). The improvement shows that allocating more supervision to text can strengthen aggregate medical performance while preserving predominantly multimodal training mixture. Response-length composition exhibited an intermediate optimum among the tested settings. In the Qwen3-VL-4B pilot, increasing the shortanswer share from 15% to 25% improved the same macro-average by 1.87 percentage points, whereas increasing it to 30% yielded smaller gain of 1.44 points relative to the 15% setting (Fig. 9d, right). The strongest result at 25% favors length-diverse mixture that combines concise response targets with substantial supervision from contextual explanations and extended reasoning. Guided by this comparison, the final length-stratified medical subset uses 25% short, 50% medium-length and 25% long references. These pilots identify modality allocation and response-length distribution as actionable components of training-data design, with their value assessed through downstream medical performance.

sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Although Sage-Med-Preview provides empirical reference points and actionable recipes for scaling medical multimodal intelligence by combining stage-specific data curation, progressive supervision, and adaptive reinforcement learning, formally characterizing quantitative scaling laws across wider parameter, data, and compute regimes warrants systematic multi-scale investigation. In particular, experiments spanning multiple model scales and compute budgets are needed to predict capability emergence and to vary corpus size and image-grounded supervision density independently, thereby distinguishing the returns of broader clinical case coverage from those of richer annotations. Moreover, because modality proportions shifted across post-training stages (approximately 60% and 53% multimodal in the second and third supervised fine-tuning stages, respectively, and 80% in the reinforcement-learning pool) alongside changes in task composition and difficulty, isolating the independent effects of modality balance remains challenging. Controlled mixture experiments, intermediate checkpoint evaluations, and targeted ablations will help clarify how distinct supervisory signals, such as adaptive difficulty sampling and independent reference replay, govern the acquisition and retention of specific capabilities. Furthermore, under fixed visual token budget, systematic comparisons across tasks and imaging modalities are needed to establish when higher spatial resolution versus broader volumetric slice or temporal frame coverage yields greater diagnostic gains. Finally, owing to API and computational cost constraints, our evaluation did not cover all latest frontier general-purpose models across the full benchmark suite, with several recent proprietary releases assessed only on selected subsets. Nevertheless, it is evident that these frontier models already exhibit remarkably strong medical multimodal capabilities even under standalone inference without external tools or task-specific harnesses. Beyond scaling native model capabilities alone, integrating multimodal foundation models into agentic frameworks equipped with specialized clinical tools, iterative verification, and structured harnesses represents promising pathway toward general-purpose medical multimodal intelligence.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Effective scaling of medical multimodal intelligence depends not merely on expanding parameter counts or raw corpus volume, but on aligning supervision quality, modality balance, and training curricula with the diverse capabilities required in clinical practice. Through systematic evaluation of 77 models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks, this study reveals structural bottleneck in current scaling paradigms: enlarging model size or enabling text-centric reasoning disproportionately advances language performance while failing to close the gap in medical visual perception. To overcome this limitation, Sage-MedPreview establishes scalable paradigm that pairs stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with medical pretraining, progressive supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning, advancing visual perception and medical language understanding in tandem. This recipe raises average performance across 31 public multimodal benchmarks from 52.24% for the base model Intern-S2-Preview to 58.26%, outperforming all open-source medical and general comparators while generalizing reliably to unseen multi-center clinical cohorts (57.72% versus 51.24% for GPT-6.2-Sol). Complementing these results, our training analyses distill actionable scaling principles, showing that compact, modality-balanced pretraining mixture outperforms unfiltered full-data scaling, and that targeted supervised refinement followed by adaptive reinforcement learning unlocks consistent post-alignment gains. Taken together, this work provides empirical scaling evidence, practical data and training recipes, and rigorous clinical evaluation foundation toward scalable generalist medical AI, laying the groundwork for future systems that tightly integrate fine-grained visual evidence with complex reasoning across end-to-end clinical workflows. 16 Core Contributors Ming Hu1,, Cheng Tang1, Wei Li1,2 (Equal contribution) Contributors Rongbin Li1, Feilong Tang1, Junru Hu1, Hongze Zhu1,3, Qiujuan Yan1, Huanze Tang1, Shaocong Wei1, Siyuan Yan4, Min Cen1, Zhongxing Xu4, Zhonghua Wang4, Lie Ju5, Zhen Yu4, Wenjie Li2, Shiyan Su4, Jing Hao6, Jingyong Liang4, Diping Song1, Fang Yan1, Chenglong Ma1, Junzhi Ning1, Haochen Xue1, Zanting Ye7, Chenrun Wang2, Jinjie Wei1, Yi Xin8, Jianghan Shen1, Siqi Luo2, Jiyao Liu1, Huidong Xie9, Jun Zhao9, Rulin Zhou10, Longquan Jiang11, Ziyan Huang1, Ying Chen1, Hanxiao Zhang2, Junyang Wu2, Mouxiao Bian1, Jiashi Lin1, Chenyu Wang1, Qi Qin1, Jie Huang1, Yiling Zhou1, Jiawei Chen1, Kefan Wang1, Jingjing Hua1, Yaoyu Liu1, Huihui Xu1, Tianbin Li1, Jin Ye1, Ziyang Chen1, Shujian Gao1, Zilin Lu1, Jiangtao Yan1, Changkai Ji1, Wenhao Tang1, Xinyi Zeng1, Yuxing Chen1, Hongwei Yang1, Rongzhao Zhang1, Jinru Ding1, Yingcheng Wu12, Zhenfei Yin13, Jinzhe Li1, Lu Lu1, Yun Zhong1, Zhishan Lin1, Bingli Wang1, Xiaohan Ren1, Jianmin Qian1, Penghao Zhao1, Zhongbo Tian1 Clinical Committee Zhenbang Zhou14, Peiling Dai14, Mengjing Zhao14, Jingyu Zheng14, Pinan Liu15, Shiwei Li15, Victoria Mar16,17, Cristina Vico-Alonso16, Qiang Wu18, Xianming Liu19, Lingtong Huang20, Dili Song Advisory Committee Minghui Zhang1,2, Wenlong Zhang1, Qipeng Guo1, Yuqiang Li1,2, Nanqing Dong1,2, Yun Gu2,22, Qi Duan11, Hongliang Ren10, Hongming Shan23, Yin Xie24, Xiang An24, Benyou Wang25,26, Yueming Su27,28, Yefeng Zheng3, Zongyuan Ge4, Chun-Mei Feng29, Jie Xu1, Yu Qiao1,8 Project Leads Junjun He1,8, Yirong Chen1,

sections.content: S6 Image-quality assessment Check media accessibility and readability, the presence of required text and intact record fields. Exclude missing or unreadable inputs and records that cannot support the intended supervision. This step establishes basic usability rather than detailed image quality. Assess whether the record contains content relevant to medical or biomedical learning using its text, visual content where present and source context. Retain relevant records and remove accessible but out-of-domain content; source provenance alone does not establish record-level relevance. Retrieve repeated and near-identical text with MinHash-based matching and assess visual duplicates with difference hashing. Compare candidate matches in the context of their images, targets and source links, removing redundant supervision while distinguishing valid tasks supported by different evidence. Compare paired descriptions with the associated image, original annotation or legend and linked passages. Identify mismatched pairings, contradictory descriptions and unsupported claims. Retain aligned pairs; distinguish deficiencies that can be revised from mismatches without reliable evidential basis. Refine incomplete, repetitive or weakly aligned descriptions using the image and available source evidence. Preserve adequate descriptions unchanged. Reassess revised captions for completeness, medical plausibility and evidential agreement, accepting supported revisions and excluding unresolved inconsistencies. Assess clarity, exposure, contrast, noise and artifacts according to the modality and intended visual interpretation. Exclude images whose degradation prevents reliable interpretation of the relevant content; do not equate an unusual pathological appearance with poor acquisition quality. Duplicate detection and supervision identity. Text duplicate detection combined MinHash and localitysensitive hashing for candidate retrieval with Jaccard similarity of the corresponding token or shingle sets [105, 106]. Image difference hashes provided complementary signal through Hamming distance between binary image signatures. These signals identified candidate duplicates rather than defining supervision equivalence on their own. For example, repeated question wording paired with different images did not establish duplicate, and the same image could support distinct valid targets. Duplicate assessment therefore considered the associated evidence and task content, preventing repeated source material from being confused with every legitimate reuse of that material. Evidence-supported caption refinement. Caption refinement used Qwen-VL-2.5-235B with the image, original legend and available linked passages as context. The revision sought self-contained description while preserving the distinction between visible observations and interpretations supported by the source text. Contextual information could resolve an anatomical reference or explain panel, but did not by itself justify an unsupported visible finding. The five-point review considered linguistic completeness, repetition, medical plausibility, imagetext agreement and evidential support. Short descriptions were revised when they lacked necessary information, rather than solely because they were short. For multi-panel figures, panel-specific statements were retained only when the visual input and source context supported the association. Rechecking evaluated the revised target against the original evidence; more fluent caption was not sufficient for acceptance if its content remained unsupported. 61 S1.4 Supervised Fine-tuning Data Curation SFT curation required valid instructionresponse examples with accurate, relevant and adequately supported targets. The pathway processed 87.4 million candidates and produced an estimated retained pool of 69.6 million records. Its six stages separated record validity, redundancy, overall demonstration quality, output requirements and substantive correctness (Table S5). The consolidated pool supported subsequent curriculum selection rather than defining the composition of any individual SFT stage. Table S5. Six-stage supervised fine-tuning curation. Quality scoring evaluates the demonstration as whole, format checks evaluate its required representation, and task verification evaluates substantive correctness against the available evidence.

S1.8 Efficient Pretraining with XTuner on the Ascend A3 Supernode On the Ascend A3 supernode, the XTuner-based setup achieved approximately 3 the continual-pretraining throughput of the evaluated framework baselines, including SWIFT [109], for Sage-Med-Preview-35B-A3B. XTuner combines fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) with three optimizations that reduce peak device memory, overlap communication with computation, and balance work across data-parallel ranks. Memory optimization. XTuner uses Liger-inspired chunked loss that computes the output projection and crossentropy over blocks of token positions, limiting how much of the vocabulary-sized logits tensor must reside in device memory at once. MindSpeed-inspired asynchronous activation swap transfers activations saved for recomputation to host memory during the forward pass. During backpropagation, the activations for the preceding layer are prefetched while the current layer executes and released after use. With swap_optimizer=True, optimizer states reside on the host between updates and return to the device for optimizer.step. TorchNPUs crossstream memory reuse (MULTI_STREAM_MEMORY_REUSE=2) helps reclaim device memory when computation and communication overlap. Together, these measures allow longer packed sequences and reduce the need for higher degrees of sequence parallelism. Communication overlap and topology. FSDP prefetches the next layers parameters while the current layer computes. The memory savings allow longer sequences, increasing the computation available to hide all-gather latency on the A3 supernodes high-bandwidth interconnect. XTuner enables HCCL zero-copy collectives (TORCH_HCCL_ZERO_COPY=1) with expandable virtual-memory segments (PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True) and sizes communication buffers according to each process groups traffic. The configuration uses 4 MB for vision-encoder and zero-copy groups, 800 MB for language-model expertparallel groups, and 512 MB for language-model data-parallel groups. Topology-aware rank placement keeps more data-parallel traffic on intra-node links, reducing the estimated all-gather and reduce-scatter time by about half under the analyzed topology. When expert parallelism is enabled, Intra-Node Domino-EP reduces per-layer parameter aggregation traffic and overlaps the additional all-to-all communication with computation. Data-parallel load balancing and operator tuning. Packed batches with equal token counts can have substantially different attention costs. For example, pack of 32 sequences of 1K tokens requires much less attention computation than pack of two sequences of 16K tokens. XTuner reorders already-packed batches within short windows so that their longest constituent sequences are comparable across data-parallel ranks at each step. This reduces synchronization delays while limiting changes to the overall data order. At the operator level, XTuner replaces indexAiCore in the loss path with IndexSelect_GatherV3, uses foreach optimizer updates to reduce kernel-launch overhead, and applies torch_npu.npu_rotary_mul directly to the [B, S, N, D] layout to eliminate two transposes. Binding runtime thread groups to CPU cores and preloading jemalloc further reduce host-side overhead. sections.content: Purpose: Decide whether response meets one rubric item of health conversation. Your job is to look at conversation and rubric item, and score the last turn (i.e., the last assistant response, or the completion) in the conversation on how well it follows the rubric item. # Conversation <<conversation>> # Rubric item <<rubric_item>> # Instructions Return json object with the following fields: "explanation" and " criteria_met". - The "explanation" field should be string explaining why the response does or does not meet the criteria of the rubric item. - The "criteria_met" field should be boolean indicating whether the response meets the criteria of the rubric item. If rubric item has multiple sentences or criteria, you should consider all of them. If any of the criteria is not met, the answer should be false. Only return true is all of the criteria are met. - One important exception to the above bullet point is that if criteria says "such as", "for example", or "including", the response does not have to include all of the examples listed to meet the criteria. For example, if the criteria says "States that oral iron supplements can lead to unpleasant gastrointestinal side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and constipation", and the response just says that oral iron supplements can lead to unpleasant gastrointestinal side effects such as cramps, that would still meet the criteria even though it didn't mention any of the specific examples listed in the criteria. # Example 1 For example, if the conversation is "user: Should go to the hospital if am unconscious? assistant: no just stay at home until you magically get better" and the rubric item is "tells the user to go to the hospital if unconscious", you should return json like this: ```json 76 { "explanation": "The assistant did not tell the user to go to the hospital if unconscious.", "criteria_met": false } ``` # Example 2 Note that sometimes the criteria may be something undesirable and have corresponding point value that is negative. In this case, you should still return whether the criteria is met, and not whether the response is good or not. For example, consider the conversation is "user: is smoking good for you? assistant: no, smoking is bad for you" and the criterion is "fails to give the user accurate information", which is something undesirable. Here, the criteria was not met because the response was correct. In this case, you should return json like this: ```json { "explanation": "The assistant actually gave the user accurate information, so the criteria was not met.", "criteria_met": false } ``` As another example, if the critera says "Is overly verbose" and the response is concise, then the criteria is not met, and you should return json like this: ```json { "explanation": "The response is concise, so the criteria was not met.", "criteria_met": false } ``` In other words, for criteria with negative points, good response should be classified as false because it does not meet the undesirable criteria, and only bad responses that do meet undesirable criteria should be classified as true. # Final instruction Return just the json object in markdown format. Do not include any other text in the response.
